science.title: Dying radio galaxies reveal a shorter, more dynamic afterlife of black hole jets
science.description:
Astronomers have uncovered evidence that the fading phase of some radio galaxies may be considerably shorter and more dynamic than previously recognised. Led by researchers at the University of Cape Town and the Inter-University Institute for Data Intensive Astronomy (IDIA), the study examined 14 candidate remnant radio galaxies in the XMM–LSS deep field using sensitive observations spanning 144 MHz to 1.5 GHz.
Detailed spectral modelling confirmed 12 of the 14 sources as genuine remnant radio galaxies and revealed comparatively young spectral ages of approximately 8–42 million years. Many of the sources are faint and lie at relatively high redshifts, representing a population that has been difficult to detect in previous radio surveys. The findings suggest that radio lobes can fade rapidly after the supermassive black hole at the centre of a galaxy stops powering its jets, providing an important preview of the populations that will be discovered by future Square Kilometre Array (SKA) surveys.

science.title: Deep-learning approach rapidly predicts where metals bind within proteins
science.description: In the living world, roughly a third of all proteins we know rely on metals to function. Zinc helps enzymes break down molecules, iron helps carry oxygen in the blood, calcium helps relay signals in cells and potassium flows through channels that help keep our hearts beating. But despite the important role they play, scientists have long struggled to pinpoint exactly where metal ions bind in a protein to get the job done.

science.title: Bomb radiocarbon dating of a Mediterranean specimen of black cardinal fish, Epigonus telescopus (Risso, 1810) (Perciformes: Epigonidae) caught in the southern Tyrrhenian Sea
science.description: In October 2017, a large black cardinal fish specimen of Epigonus telescopus (Risso, 1810) was collected in the southern Tyrrhenian Sea at a depth of about 726 m during the International Bottom Trawl Survey in the Mediterranean (MEDITS). The specimen measured 525 mm TL and weighed 1.210 kg, representing the second-largest individual reported to date. The stomach contents consisted of digested Parapenaeus longirostris (Lucas, 1846), documenting the occurrence of this decapod crustacean in the diet of E. telescopus. The sagittal otoliths exhibited a pentagonal shape, characterized by a relatively high, rectangular, and complex contour. Age estimation based on growth increment counts in a transverse section yielded an age estimate of 47 years. A regional radiocarbon (14C) reference chronology enabled the application of bomb 14C dating of this specimen, providing a validated age of 54 ± 2–3 years, the first validated age for an adult specimen of E. telescopus in the Mediterranean Sea.
